\chapter{Review --- Four Things Worth Saying Twice}
\label{ch:repaso-pre-a1}
\hlchaptermodality{318}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say goodbye for the short term, pick the right sorry, and say which noun's ending is lying to me.}

Complete ES-C318-repaso-genero: place la cabeza, el vino and la mano by gender, then use the object pronoun to settle el agua.

\section[(review)]{Review — hasta pronto, and the word inside it}

\label{lesson:ES-C318-repaso-despedirse}



\begin{quote}
Two words, and you have had both for a long time. What does \emph{hasta} mean? (\textbf{Until}.) And \emph{pronto}? (\textbf{Soon} — and also \textquotedblleft{}quickly\textquotedblright{}, and \textquotedblleft{}ready\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Say it once, slowly: \textbf{hasta pronto}, \emph{AHS-tah PRON-toh}. \textquotedblleft{}Until soon.\textquotedblright{}

Now take the second half on its own. \textbf{Pronto} came from Latin \textbf{promptus}, \textquotedblleft{}brought forth, ready at hand\textquotedblright{}. Something \emph{prompt} is brought out without delay — and that is the whole distance between \textquotedblleft{}ready\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}soon\textquotedblright{}.

English has the same word, unchanged in the root: \textbf{prompt}, \textbf{promptly}, and the computer \textbf{prompt} that sits there ready for you to type. Italian took it too, and says \emph{\textbf{Pronto!}} — \textquotedblleft{}Ready!\textquotedblright{} — when it answers the phone.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hasta pronto}, then \emph{pronto} on its own
  \item \emph{pronto}, then English \emph{prompt}, \emph{promptly} — one word, two languages
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of your goodbyes says you expect to meet again shortly? (\emph{\textbf{Hasta pronto}}.) And what is \emph{pronto} on its own? (\textbf{Soon}, and \textquotedblleft{}ready\textquotedblright{} — the sense English kept in \emph{prompt}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — two sorries, and how to tell them apart}

\label{lesson:ES-C318-repaso-disculparse}



\begin{quote}
What does \textbf{lo siento} say, word for word? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I feel it\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{siento} from Latin \emph{sentīre}, \textquotedblleft{}to feel\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
English has one word where Spanish has two, and the split follows the etymologies you already hold.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{phrase} & \textbf{word for word} & \textbf{points at} \\
\midrule
\textbf{lo siento} & \textquotedblleft{}I feel it\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{your} feeling \\
\textbf{perdón} & \textquotedblleft{}give {[}it{]} completely\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{their} forgiveness \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Lo siento} names a feeling — regret, sympathy — and stretches from stepping on a foot to hearing that someone has died. \emph{Perdón} asks for something back, which is why it is also what you say squeezing past a stranger in a corridor.

Be honest about the edges, as the first pass was: speakers reach for whichever fits, the boundary is soft, and mixing them is a shade off rather than a mistake.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{lo siento}, then \emph{perdón} — feeling, then request
  \item \emph{lo siento mucho} — I feel it a lot
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which one leans toward sympathy rather than fault? (\emph{\textbf{Lo siento}}.) Which one is asking the other person for something? (\emph{\textbf{Perdón}} — a pardon is a thing granted.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — four nouns, easiest gender to hardest}

\label{lesson:ES-C318-repaso-genero}



\begin{quote}
Two you can answer without thinking. Say \textquotedblleft{}the head.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{La cabeza}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}the wine.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{El vino}}.) The ending told you both times.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Line up four nouns you already own, in order of how much the ending can be trusted.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{noun} & \textbf{ending} & \textbf{gender} \\
\midrule
\textbf{la cabeza} & \emph{-a} & feminine, as expected \\
\textbf{el vino} & \emph{-o} & masculine, as expected \\
\textbf{la mano} & \emph{-o} & \textbf{feminine} anyway \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Cabeza} and \emph{vino} are the ordinary case, and they are worth saying out loud precisely because nothing about them is interesting: the ending points one way and the article agrees.

\textbf{La mano} is the famous one. Latin \textbf{manus} sat in the fourth declension, whose \emph{-us} nouns were mostly masculine — and \emph{manus} was one of the handful that were feminine instead. So it broke the pattern twice: once inside Latin, and once again against Spanish's usual \emph{-o}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: when the ending will not tell you}]
The fourth noun is the one where even the \textbf{article} is unhelpful.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Bebo \textbf{el agua}.} — I drink the water. \emph{\textbf{La} bebo.} — I drink it.
\end{quote}

The article said \emph{el} to keep two \emph{a} sounds from colliding, which is a fact about sound and not about gender. The object pronoun is under no such pressure, so it reports the gender straight — and it reports \textbf{la}.

That is a test you can run on any noun whose article looks suspicious: listen for which pronoun a speaker reaches for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cabeza}, \emph{el vino}, \emph{la mano} — two obedient, one not
  \item \emph{el agua}, then \emph{la bebo} — the article, then the witness
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four nouns ends in \emph{-o} and is feminine anyway? (\emph{\textbf{La mano}}.) \emph{El agua} — which pronoun replaces it? (\emph{\textbf{La}}.) And why does that not contradict the article? (The article changed for \textbf{sound}, not gender.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — two marks that were added, and when}

\label{lesson:ES-C318-repaso-marcas}



\begin{quote}
Why does Spanish open a question with \textbf{¿}? (Because the \textbf{words do not move} — so the reader needs an early warning to lift their voice.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The \textbf{¿} is younger than the language, and it has a date.

The Spanish Royal Academy made the opening mark official in \textbf{1754}. English can usually tell you a question is coming by reordering the words — \emph{Are} you…, \emph{Do} you… — so its final \textbf{?} arrives late and costs nothing. Spanish does not reorder: \emph{Tienes hambre} and \emph{¿Tienes hambre?} are the same words. Something had to carry the warning, and the Academy put it at the front.

A melody cue placed \textbf{before} the melody. That is the whole idea, and it is the same instinct as the written accent showing a stress you could not otherwise see.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Now the second mark, and it is quieter.

Latin \textbf{germānus} is stressed on its third syllable, which leaves the opening \emph{ger-} unstressed — and there the \textbf{g} simply fell away, giving Old Spanish \emph{\textbf{ermano}}, with no \emph{h} at all. The \emph{h} on today's \textbf{hermano} was added later, in spelling only, to point back at the Latin \emph{g-}.

Keep it apart from the other silent \emph{h}. In \textbf{hijo} and \textbf{hacer} the \emph{h} stands where Latin had an \emph{f}, and that \emph{h} really was breathed aloud for centuries. \emph{Hermano}'s never was. Same silent letter, two histories, and only one of them ever involved a sound.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{germānus}, then \emph{ermano}, then \emph{hermano} — the three stages
  \item a question of your own, and start lifting your voice where the ¿ sits
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What year did the Academy make \textbf{¿} official? (\textbf{1754}.) And what happened to \emph{germānus}'s opening letter? (Its \textbf{g} dropped away in an unstressed syllable — the \emph{h} was put on the page afterwards, and never spoken.)
\end{tcolorbox}
